name: NAURU
lead: Nauru is the world's smallest republic — a coral dot in the Pacific barely bigger than 1,000 football pitches. Sailors called it Pleasant Island. Its soil turned out to be phosphate — ancient seabird droppings — making it one of the richest places on Earth. Today Nauruans rebuild among jagged limestone left by the mines.

sections.geography: A coral dot in the Pacific

geo: Nauru is a flat oval of raised coral reef, ringed by a narrow coastal strip where almost everyone lives. Inland, a central plateau sits about 30 metres up — once covered in phosphate-rich soil, now largely bare limestone after a century of mining.

The island has no rivers and almost no freshwater except Buada Lagoon, a quiet inland pond fringed with palms. The ocean drops to great depths just offshore, making for spectacular reef diving right on its fringe.
animals: Nauru's most famous resident is the Nauru reed warbler — a small brown bird found nowhere else on Earth. It hops through remaining scrub hunting insects with its thin beak. Mining destroyed most of its forest home, making it vulnerable.

Great frigatebirds swoop above the coast, riding warm currents to snatch fish mid-flight. Beneath the waves, colourful reef fish, sea turtles, and trevally dart around coral. Open-ocean wanderers like tuna pass just offshore.
culture: Nauruans belong to 12 ancient clans, each with its own stories. Descent is traced through mothers — your clan follows your mum's family. Feasts bring everyone together around fresh fish, coconut, and pandanus fruit.

Traditional chants and dances keep old stories alive. Woven pandanus mats and baskets are skills passed down through generations. Weightlifting is a proudly national sport; Nauruan athletes have won Olympic medals in it.
history: Micronesian settlers arrived around 1000 BCE. In 1798 British captain John Fearn called it Pleasant Island. Germany claimed it in 1888; Britain, Australia, and Japan each controlled it at different points during both world wars.

Phosphate mining began in 1907 and made Nauru the world's richest country per capita by the 1970s. Reserves ran dry by the early 2000s, leaving 80% of the land stripped bare. Nauru has been independent since 1968.
wows: Nauru is the world's smallest independent republic — only Vatican City and Monaco are tinier.
You can drive around the entire island in about 20 minutes on the one ring road.
Nauru's phosphate formed from millions of years of seabird droppings — wealth built on ancient poo.
In the 1970s Nauru had one of the highest incomes per person on Earth, funding its own airline.
Nauru has no official capital; government offices sit in Yaren, the closest thing to a main town.
Only around 200 tourists visit Nauru each year — one of the lowest figures of any country on Earth.
Each of the 12 points on the flag's star stands for one of Nauru's 12 original clans.

myths.myth: Nauru is still a rich, prosperous island
myths.fact: Nauru was fabulously wealthy in the 1970s–80s from phosphate. When the mines ran dry, so did the money. Today it is rebuilding its economy and restoring mined-out land.

myths.myth: The interior is lush tropical jungle
myths.fact: Mining stripped 80% of the island bare, leaving jagged limestone spikes. Wildlife inland is sparse; the main land bird is the vulnerable Nauru reed warbler.
